862.title: The bodhi tree cutting
862.hook: Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta brings a cutting of the bodhi tree to Anuradhapura, where it still grows
862.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit the bodhi tree at Anuradhapura to offer flowers and water and to sit in meditation, and Sri Lankan Buddhists remember Sanghamitta's arrival at a full moon festival each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahinda, a monk on a rock and a riddle about a mango tree. Your line: the teaching crossed the sea.

On the island, a group of women have a request. Anula, a woman of the royal house, and the women around her have heard Mahinda teach, and they want to be ordained as nuns. Mahinda says he can't: the chronicle has him say it isn't allowed for monks to ordain women. That takes nuns, and there are no nuns on the island. But Mahinda has a sister. So a message goes back across the sea to the emperor, asking for two things: his daughter, and a branch of a tree.
screen: `THE WOMEN ASK TO BE ORDAINED.` → `NO NUNS ON THE ISLAND.` → `SEND FOR A SISTER.`

segments.voice: First, the sister. Sanghamitta is a nun, Ashoka's daughter, and in the Mahavamsa she agrees to go. She can give the island's women what they asked for. Second, the branch. It comes from the bodhi tree, under which the Buddha sat the night he awoke. The chronicle tells of a branch taken with great ceremony and set in a golden vessel, carried to the coast and onto a ship, with Sanghamitta beside it: music, offerings, the sea itself, it says, made calm. Third, the arrival. When the ship comes in, King Devanampiya Tissa wades into the water up to his neck to receive the branch. There's the image: a king, soaked, holding a pot with a tree in it over his head. The branch is carried to the royal capital, Anuradhapura, and planted in a park there. And Anula and the women around her are ordained by Sanghamitta. The tree and the nuns arrive together. Fourth, it still grows. At Anuradhapura today, a bodhi tree stands behind railings, held up by props, surrounded by flags and pilgrims. Tradition holds that it is that same tree, grown from the branch Sanghamitta brought. Pilgrims sit near it, offer flowers, and pour water at its roots. Historians may ask what can be proven. The people beneath it honor something simpler: a living thing cared for by many hands, for a very long time.
screen: `A SISTER WHO CAN ORDAIN.` · `A BRANCH IN A GOLDEN VESSEL.` · `THE KING WADES INTO THE SEA.` · `IT STILL GROWS.`

Then let it keep you company while you sit, something alive and slowly growing while you stay still.

863.title: Written down
863.hook: in the first century BCE the Pali canon was written on palm leaves at Aluvihara
863.howItsDone: Theravada monasteries keep both ways alive: monks memorize and chant the texts together, and the written canon, once kept on palm leaves, is now printed and studied as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sanghamitta, a branch in a golden vessel and a king wading into the sea. Your line: it still grows.

A strip of dried palm leaf, long and narrow, lies across a monk's knee. He scratches letters into it with a metal stylus, line after careful line. Later, soot and oil are rubbed across the leaf and wiped away, and the dark stays only in the scratches, so the words appear. A whole library can be made this way, one leaf at a time, tied between wooden boards. In Sri Lanka, the chronicle says, there came a day when the monks decided the teaching had to be written down in books.
screen: `A STRIP OF PALM LEAF.` → `A STYLUS SCRATCHES LETTERS.` → `THE MONKS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: First, a teaching that lived in voices. Monks learned the discourses and the rules by heart and chanted them together, so one person's mistake could be caught by the others. The chronicles of Sri Lanka say the three baskets of the teaching, and the commentaries on them, had been handed down that way, by mouth. Second, the fear. The Mahavamsa sets this moment in the reign of King Vattagamani, a troubled reign in which the king himself is driven from his throne for a time. The monks saw that people were falling away, the chronicle says, so they came together and wrote the texts down in books, that the true teaching might endure. That's the whole reason it gives. Not convenience. Survival. Third, the place. Tradition names it as Aluvihara, a monastery among great rocks, and pilgrims still visit. Fourth, what changed and what didn't. Writing didn't end the chanting. Monks still learn texts by heart and recite them together, and in monasteries today the voice is still one way the teaching is received. But now there was a second, quieter keeper: leaves in a bundle, waiting for anyone who could read. When a manuscript wore out, it could be copied fresh. That's how a text stays alive, the way a tree does: not by never changing, but by being renewed. The monks at Aluvihara didn't know who would read their leaves. They wrote for strangers, so the teaching wouldn't depend on any one memory, or any one life.
screen: `A TEACHING THAT LIVED IN VOICES.` · `AFRAID IT COULD BE LOST.` · `WRITTEN AT ALUVIHARA.` · `CHANTING GOES ON.`

864.title: The stupas
864.hook: Sanchi and Bharhut: great mounds holding relics, walked around clockwise
864.howItsDone: At stupas and pagodas, Buddhist pilgrims walk clockwise, sometimes three times, sometimes chanting or carrying flowers and incense, as an act of respect and meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the teaching written down, so it would endure. Your line: on palm leaves.

A dome of brick and stone, rounded like an upturned bowl, rises from a hilltop in central India. Around it runs a stone railing, and through the railing, carved gateways crowded with elephants, trees and people, whole stories in relief. Pilgrims don't go inside. There is no inside to go to. They walk around it, slowly, always in the same direction. This is the great stupa at Sanchi. Today's word is the shape itself.
screen: `A DOME LIKE AN UPTURNED BOWL.` → `CARVED GATEWAYS.` → `NO INSIDE. THEY WALK AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha's own instruction. In the Great Discourse on the final passing, Ananda asks what should be done with the Teacher's body. Treat it like the remains of a great king, the Buddha answers, and build a stupa where four roads meet. Whoever brings a garland or scent there, or bows, or simply grows calm in heart, it will be for their good and happiness for a long time. Second, the relics shared. After the cremation, the discourse says, the peoples who had loved him each asked for a share of the remains and built a stupa over theirs. So from the start, a stupa is a mound with something precious sealed at its heart, out of sight. Third, Sanchi and Bharhut. Their stone railings and gateways survive, covered with carvings: the Jataka tales, scenes from the Buddha's life, spirits of the trees, ordinary people bringing offerings. Some carvings carry the names of those who paid for them, monks, nuns, merchants, villagers, their small gifts cut into the stone. Fourth, walking around it. Pilgrims circle a stupa keeping it on their right, which means clockwise, an old Indian gesture of respect. In the suttas, visitors often leave the Buddha the same way, keeping him on their right. At a stupa, the whole visit is that gesture, again and again. The body moves; the center stays still. And the walk becomes the prayer, or the meditation, or simply a way of saying: this matters, and I came.
screen: `A MOUND WHERE FOUR ROADS MEET.` · `THE RELICS SHARED OUT.` · `GATEWAYS FULL OF STORIES.` · `KEEP IT ON YOUR RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Choose something near you, a table, a chair, a plant, and walk slowly around it once, keeping it on your right and feeling each foot land; if walking isn't possible today, trace the circle with your eyes or your hand. When you're back where you began, bow your head a little if it feels right, and let the circle settle with the breath.

865.title: The empty throne
865.hook: early art showed the Buddha by symbols only: a footprint, a wheel, a tree, an empty seat
865.howItsDone: Buddhists still honor the Buddha through symbols like the wheel of dhamma, carved footprints and the bodhi tree, alongside statues, and pilgrims bow and leave offerings before them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stupa, a mound with relics at its heart, and pilgrims circling it. Your line: walk around it. Today, back to the carved gateways for a closer look.

On a carved stone panel, a crowd has gathered. People kneel with their hands together; some hold flowers. Above them spreads a great tree, every leaf cut into the stone, and beneath it is a seat, a throne with a cushion. Everyone faces it, bowing. And the seat is empty. On panel after panel of the old railings and gateways, the scene repeats. The Buddha's life is everywhere in the stone, and the Buddha, it seems, is nowhere.
screen: `A CROWD KNEELS.` → `A TREE, A SEAT.` → `THE SEAT IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: First, the signs. In the carvings at places like Bharhut and Sanchi, the Buddha's great moments are shown, but not him, at least not as a human figure. The awakening is a tree with an empty seat beneath it. The first teaching is a wheel, the wheel of dhamma set turning. His presence is a pair of footprints, or a parasol held over no one. A riderless horse leaves the palace. Every story is there, and at its center is a space. Second, the one who has gone out. The suttas don't describe these carvings, but one passage sits beside them well. In the Sutta Nipata, a seeker named Upasiva asks the Buddha what becomes of one who has reached the end. The Buddha answers with a flame. A flame blown out by the wind comes to rest and can't be counted any more. So with the sage: there's no measure for him, nothing left by which to say he is this or that. Some readers see the empty seat as that teaching in stone. Third, the other reading. Some scholars suggest that some of these scenes show later pilgrims worshiping at the holy places, the tree, the seat, the footprints, rather than the Buddha's own moments with him left out. Serious people hold both readings, and the stone itself doesn't settle it. Fourth, what the absence does. Either way, a visitor to these panels can't stare at a face. You look at what he left: a teaching, a path, a place where someone sat down and woke up. The seat is left open.
screen: `A TREE, A WHEEL, A FOOTPRINT.` · `NO MEASURE FOR ONE GONE OUT.` · `SCHOLARS READ IT TWO WAYS.` · `THE SEAT IS LEFT OPEN.`

segments.voice: With a pen on paper, or a finger on your palm, slowly draw one of the old signs: a circle with spokes for the wheel, the outline of a footprint, or a small square seat with nothing on it. Don't make it good; make it slow. Then look at the empty part, the space inside the lines, and let that space be enough while you breathe.

866.title: The first images
866.hook: in Gandhara and Mathura, the first statues of the Buddha appear
866.howItsDone: Buddhists today bow before images of the Buddha and offer flowers, candles and incense, and the wheel and footprint remain in use beside them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asana, the empty seat, the Buddha shown by what he left. Your line: shown by absence. Today, someone sits down.

Two statues stand in a museum, a few steps apart. Both are the Buddha. The first is carved in gray stone: wavy hair, a calm face, a heavy robe falling in deep folds over both shoulders, a body that looks as if it could breathe. The second is reddish stone: a rounder face, broad shoulders, one shoulder bare, a slight smile, a hand raised with the palm out. They come from two different regions, Gandhara and Mathura. After the empty seat, the Buddha has a face. In fact, he has two.
screen: `TWO STATUES.` → `GRAY STONE, RED STONE.` → `THE BUDDHA HAS A FACE.`

segments.voice: First, Gandhara. In the northwest, where trade roads crossed and many peoples met, carvers made Buddhas with flowing hair and robes in deep, rippling folds. Art historians see in them the touch of Greek and Roman sculpture, which had reached that region. The Buddha stands like a figure from a classical temple, but his eyes are lowered, and he is still. Second, Mathura. Further south and east, carvers in the city of Mathura worked in a reddish sandstone. Their Buddhas are fuller, broad-chested, often smiling, in a thin robe that clings to the body: strong, present, ready to speak. Third, the question nobody can settle. Which came first? Scholars have argued for a long time and still disagree. Some look to Gandhara, some to Mathura, and some think the two began around the same time. It's honest to leave it open. Fourth, the signs that stayed. Whatever the style, the new images carried marks that meant something: a rise on the crown of the head, a small mark between the eyebrows, long earlobes, stretched, tradition says, by the heavy earrings of the prince he once was. And one hand raised, palm out, in the gesture often read as do not fear. The empty seat had said: he is gone beyond measure. The statue says: he was here, and this is what a calm human being can look like. Buddhist art goes on holding both. The images didn't replace the wheel and the footprint. They sat down beside them.
screen: `GANDHARA: WAVY HAIR, DEEP FOLDS.` · `MATHURA: RED STONE, A SMILE.` · `WHICH CAME FIRST? STILL DEBATED.` · `THE HAND THAT SAYS DO NOT FEAR.`

Then close your eyes and see if any of that stillness can settle into your own face and hands.

867.title: The Greek king's questions
867.hook: King Menander, a Greek ruler in India, questions the monk Nagasena (Milinda, Book 2)
867.howItsDone: Theravada monks and students read the Questions of King Milinda as a guide to hard questions, and teachers still retell its similes, like the chariot, when explaining the teaching on self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gandhara and Mathura, and a face in stone. Your line: a face appears. Today, a voice: a king who wants answers.

A king rides out of his city with a crowd of courtiers, restless for a debate. The book that tells his story calls him clever and fond of argument, a man who has questioned teacher after teacher and left each one tongue-tied. Nobody, his courtiers admit, can stand up to him anymore. Then someone mentions a monk who has just arrived, named Nagasena. The king goes to see him. His name is Milinda in the Pali book, and historians link him with Menander, a Greek ruler in the northwest of India. The book is called the Questions of King Milinda.
screen: `A KING WHO WINS EVERY ARGUMENT.` → `A MONK NAMED NAGASENA.` → `THE QUESTIONS OF KING MILINDA.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. The book opens in Sagala, a rich city of parks, gates and markets, which it places in the country of the Yonakas, the Greeks. So the conversation is a meeting of two worlds: a Greek king and a Buddhist monk, talking in India. Second, the ground rules. Early on, the king asks whether Nagasena will keep discussing with him. Yes, says Nagasena, if the king talks as a scholar talks; no, if he talks as a king talks. What's the difference? Scholars explain and are explained to, correct and are corrected, and don't get angry about it. Kings state a view, and whoever disagrees is punished. The king agrees to talk as a scholar. Third, the questions. They are not polite. Who keeps the precepts, if there is no self? Is the one who is reborn the same person or someone else? If the Buddha was free of every bad deed, why did he ever feel pain? The king asks what a skeptic would ask, and the book lets him ask it at full strength. Fourth, why this matters. The Theravada tradition kept this book and still teaches from it. So a text Buddhists value is built out of an outsider's hardest questions, asked in good faith and answered patiently, with the king's doubts in plain view. Over the next days come Nagasena's answers, one at a time: a chariot, a flame, a stolen mango, a pot of milk.
screen: `SAGALA: A GREEK KING IN INDIA.` · `TALK AS A SCHOLAR, NOT AS A KING.` · `HARD QUESTIONS, ASKED AT FULL STRENGTH.` · `A TREASURED BOOK OF AN OUTSIDER'S QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `CORRECT AND BE CORRECTED.`

segments.voice: Think of something you honestly don't understand, about this path, about someone in your life, about yourself: not a trap, a real question. Say it to yourself plainly, the way the king might, and notice how it feels to hold a question without rushing to win it.
Milinda. The king of the Questions of King Milinda, linked by historians with the Greek ruler Menander, who asks the monk Nagasena everything.

868.title: The chariot
868.hook: is the chariot the axle, the wheels, the pole? "Nagasena" is a name for parts together (Milinda, Book 2)
868.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the chariot simile from the Questions of King Milinda, together with the nun Vajira's verse, to explain not-self: a name is used for parts working together, with no fixed core behind them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Milinda meets Nagasena. Your line: the king's questions. This week the teaching took root: a bodhi cutting that still grows, a canon on palm leaves, stupas, an empty throne, a first face in stone, and a king with questions.

The king asks the simplest question there is: what's your name? The monk's answer surprises the court. He's called Nagasena, he says; that's what his parents and fellow monks call him. But it's only a name, a way of speaking. No lasting person is found behind it. The king turns to his courtiers, half amused, half offended. If there's no person here, who wears these robes? Who keeps the rules? Who gets the credit when someone gives alms, and who's to blame if someone harms you? Nagasena doesn't argue. He asks the king how he got here today.
screen: `WHAT'S YOUR NAME?` → `ONLY A NAME, A WAY OF SPEAKING.` → `THEN WHO WEARS THE ROBES?`

segments.voice: First, the chariot at the door. The king came by chariot, so Nagasena asks him to point to it. Is the pole the chariot? No. The axle? The wheels? The frame, the yoke, the reins? No, no, no. All of these together? No. Something apart from them? No again. Second, the turn. Then there is no chariot, Nagasena says, and the king has told a falsehood in front of his court. The courtiers cheer for the monk. And the king, to his credit, works it out aloud. He hasn't lied: chariot is the name used for the pole, the axle, the wheels, the frame and the rest, when they come together. Third, the point. Just so, Nagasena says: Nagasena is the name for this body, these feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness, when they come together. Nothing is hidden behind the parts; the name is real as a name. He recalls a verse of the nun Vajira, from the older suttas: where the parts are gathered, people say chariot; where the parts of a life are present, people say a being. The king praises the answer. Fourth, what this doesn't say. It doesn't say Nagasena isn't there, or that names are lies. The king still rides home in his chariot. A name points to parts working together, not to a fixed core inside them. Buddhists call this anatta, not-self, and this simile is one of the ways teachers still explain it.
screen: `IS THE POLE THE CHARIOT? THE WHEELS?` · `THE KING WORKS IT OUT ALOUD.` · `NAGASENA: A NAME FOR PARTS TOGETHER.` · `THE CHARIOT STILL CARRIES HIM HOME.` · then, large: `A NAME FOR PARTS.`

segments.voice: Pick something near you, a cup, a chair, a phone, and name its parts slowly: the handle, the rim, the base. Where among them is the cup itself? Then gently turn the same question toward your own name, a body breathing, feelings coming and going, thoughts, and just watch the parts working together, with no conclusion needed.
The chariot. Nagasena's simile: not the pole, not the wheels, nothing apart from them; chariot is a name for the parts together.
Your line: a name for parts. The chariot still gets the king home. Day eight hundred sixty-eight, and another week behind us.
